source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough
finding: CaRT fine-tunes a small model on counterfactual pairs of trajectories (one where stopping is right, one minimally edited where it is not) plus written reasons. It beat the base model and plain SFT on stop timing in medical diagnosis dialogues.
numbers: Medical arm: train 1,133 problems (MedQA-USMLE + MedMCQA, GPT-4o-simulated dialogues); test 100 in-distribution + 200 dermatology OOD. Model Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Labels: Llama-3.1-8B success over 50 generations per prefix. Optimal stop = first turn where success rises by at least 0.5. CIs over 3 training seeds and 30 eval runs. Exact bar values are only in figures, not in the text.
limits: Single lab, no independent replication found. Training data and simulated patient both come from LLMs. Small models only (1.7B to 3B). Success is oracle-labelled by another LLM, not by clinicians.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that 'know enough' can be trained. Our agent cannot fine-tune, so the transferable part is the contrast: ask what would make stopping wrong next to what makes it right (S8).

source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough (math arm)
finding: In math, CaRT decides after each reasoning episode whether to stop thinking. It reached higher AIME 2025 success with fewer thinking tokens than base and SFT. RL on top (GRPO) gave longer traces and no gain in math.
numbers: Train: 2,000 DeepScaleR problems, Qwen3-1.7B trajectories, 10 episode prefixes each. Eval AIME 2025, 3 seeds x 16 evals. Label 'terminate' if stopping early beats continuing. Exact values only in Fig. 4.
limits: Tiny model, one hard benchmark (30 problems). Stop test is a forced answer from a truncated prefix, so it measures answer-from-prefix, not a live stop.
agent_relevance: The stop label 'forced answer now beats continuing' can be computed by code on a sampled prefix. Fits our S0 and S8 idea of a code-checked stop.

source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough (ablation)
finding: Counterfactual data gave the largest gain; reasoning traces added a smaller consistent gain. Plain SFT learned a crude heuristic: stop more as the dialogue gets longer. Counterfactuals made stopping spike at the true information jumps; reasoning smoothed the curve.
numbers: Ablations: CaRT, -reason, -CF, -CF-reason, and SFT with 5/10/15/20% terminate ratio. A verbalised confidence ('diagnosis: 30%') helped SFT and SFT+CF but gave no significant gain on full CaRT. In math, Qwen3-1.7B without counterfactuals did worse than the fixed-budget baseline.
limits: Ablations shown as Pareto plots; no p-values in the text. The reasoning gain may depend on the 3B model.
agent_relevance: Stopping by position or length is the default failure. Any stop rule must depend on content gain, not turn count.

source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough (OOD and probe)
finding: On out-of-distribution dermatology cases the base model and plain SFT did worse than a naive fixed-stop baseline; CaRT stayed above it with a smaller margin. Probe on 102 counterfactual conversations: direct accuracy base 0.567, CaRT without reasons 0.849, full CaRT 0.663; logistic probe test accuracy 0.581, 0.645, 0.774.
numbers: 102 conversations, 70/30 split, so about 31 test items. CI for full CaRT probe test accuracy 0.602 to 0.886.
limits: Probe test set is tiny and CIs overlap; the authors say so. PDF text extraction scrambled the table rows; I assigned them using the paper's statement that SFT+CF has the highest direct accuracy.
agent_relevance: A learned stop rule can be worse than a fixed rule after domain shift. Check any stop rule against a fixed baseline per problem class (G7).

source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM Agents to Know When They Know Enough (limits and RL)
finding: Authors say termination quality depends on how good the earlier questions were, and that what to ask and when to stop should be learned together. RL after SFT tended toward longer conversations and gave no gain in math.
numbers: Limitations from section 6; no replication. Hyperparameters in appendix.
limits: Appendix still has a leftover '[FILL IN evidence]' note for the question-asking SFT check, so one setup claim is unsupported in the text.
agent_relevance: Treat CaRT as a single-source result [S] until others reproduce it.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling answers when a Dirichlet-based test says the leading answer will stay the leader. Large cost cut, near-zero accuracy loss, no training.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 models, max 40 samples (50 to 100 for code). Sample cuts up to 7.9x, mean accuracy drop under 0.1%. By model: GPT-3.5-turbo 4.4x, Vicuna-13B 1.9x, Codex 3.4x fewer samples. By task: math 3.3x (-0.1 pt), commonsense 2.9x (-0.2), symbolic 3.8x (0), code 2.4x (+0.4).
limits: Needs repeated sampling. The stop test treats samples as independent draws, which our G4 says they are not, so its confidence is overstated.
agent_relevance: A code-run stop rule over answer counts is cheap. Use a stricter threshold than the paper because of correlated samples.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency (threshold analysis)
finding: Accuracy rises then plateaus as the confidence threshold rises, while sample count climbs steeply near the plateau. At equal average sample cost, adaptive beat fixed-budget self-consistency. A Beta stopping criterion worked; a plain majority-lead criterion did worse.
numbers: Sweep of the threshold from 0.5 to 1 on GSM8K and Date Understanding; values in figures. Worked example: 9 of the first 10 samples agree gives over 99% chance the majority stays the leader after 40 samples.
limits: The 99% figure is a model estimate, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Shape of the stop-versus-cost curve: the last points of confidence are the expensive ones.

source: Li, Yuan, Feng, et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Sample in small windows; stop when all answers in a window agree. Cuts samples a lot with similar accuracy. Also gives a control scheme to pick window size and max samples for a cost-accuracy target.
numbers: Average sample reduction: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Window 5 (8 for MATH). Averaged over 10 runs. Plain SC at the same average sample count loses accuracy, so ESC wins at equal cost.
limits: Headline cuts are against a large max budget. Saving is smaller on the hard set (MATH -33.8%). Variance not reported in the text.
agent_relevance: Simplest training-free termination rule: stop drawing attempts when the last 2 to 4 agree (S3 to S7), subject to G4.

source: Li et al. (2024) ESC (cost and combination)
finding: ESC can be combined with other reasoning methods and cuts dollar cost, because windows share one prompt. Paper claims almost no loss when applied on top of other advanced methods.
numbers: Paper's example: full SC with 64 samples on MATH with GPT-4 costs about 2,000 USD. Tables list tokens per item, cost per item and accuracy.
limits: Dollar figures depend on 2023-24 prices. Only the conservative rule (all answers in the window identical) was recommended.
agent_relevance: Supports a conservative rule: stop only on full agreement inside a window.

source: Zhang, Chen, Pan, et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States
finding: A small probe on hidden states at intermediate-answer positions predicts whether the answer is correct and is well calibrated. Using it to exit early cut tokens about 24% with no accuracy loss.
numbers: In-distribution probe ROC-AUC above 0.7, ECE below 0.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B above 0.9 AUC on AIME. Early exit: threshold 0.85 gives 88.2% accuracy (same as no exit) with about 24% fewer tokens; threshold 0.9 gives 88.6% with 19% fewer. At matched tokens the probe beat static exit by up to 5 points (87.4% vs about 82.5% at threshold 0.8).
limits: Needs hidden states, so open-weight models only. Probe does not generalise from logic to math. On AIME, probes trained on GSM8K and MATH were less calibrated.
agent_relevance: The information needed to stop exists inside the model but is unused. We cannot read hidden states from an API model, so we proxy with answer agreement (G4 caveat).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) probing (future-answer finding)
finding: Hidden states before an intermediate answer is written already predict whether it will be correct, so a stop could come before the answer is formed.
numbers: Shown as early-prediction curves on GSM8K, MATH, AIME and KnowLogic; per-position AUC values not recorded from the text I read.
limits: Per-position numbers not extracted. Same open-weight limit.
agent_relevance: A cheap stop signal exists, but only inside model weights.

source: Yang, Si, Duan, et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: At reasoning transition points (e.g. 'Wait') force a trial answer and stop if the model is confident in it. Training-free. Shortened chains and often raised accuracy.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 reasoning models. CoT length down 19.1% to 80.1% on average, accuracy up 0.3 to 5.0 points. Math and science compress 61.5% on average, code only 19.9%. Example set averages: 83.55 vanilla vs 84.45 DEER; 43.35 vs 51.05 on another set. QwQ-32B still got 19.1% shorter despite end-of-thinking token problems.
limits: Many early-exit attempts fail at early positions, which explains uneven savings. Weak gains on Llama-3.1-Nemotron-Nano-8B (low confidence). Needs token confidence and open weights. Authors chose the benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Closest prompt-level analogue to S4/S8: force a trial answer and stop on confidence. Trial answers are also harvestable (S4).

source: Yang et al. (2025) DEER (failure analysis)
finding: Weaknesses: plain confidence averaging does not fix false positives; length-prompt baselines fail on hard AIME24; for QwQ-32B some baselines break because the end-of-thinking delimiter fires unreliably.
numbers: Appendix: inconsistent answers between two approaches can leave no final answer. No quantified false-stop rate in the text I read.
limits: Stated as limitations by the authors.
agent_relevance: Premature stop is a real failure mode. Run the S8 check after the stop, and keep G6 (never abstain) for the no-answer case.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Reasoning models typically reach their final answer after about 60% of their reasoning steps. Three inference-time stop methods: answer consistency, raising end-of-thinking probability, and a learned stop probe on activations.
numbers: 5 benchmarks, 5 open models. NQ: answer consistency cuts over 40% of tokens and raises accuracy; Learn-to-Stop up to 48% on NQ (46.2% for R1-Qwen-7B vs 47.7% for another size). Another run: 44% fewer tokens (755.1 to 418.9) at 0.2% accuracy drop; GPQA 39.2% fewer tokens at similar accuracy. Consistency window k: 20 to 30 near-saturated accuracy; 10 to 20 balances cost.
limits: Smaller gains on hard tasks (MATH-500, GPQA, AIME): the authors say plain output consistency may be insufficient there.
agent_relevance: Cheap stop rule: stop when the last k probed answers agree. Larger k is safer but costs more tokens.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence (stop-quality taxonomy)
finding: Classifying where the learned stopper stops relative to the ideal point: most stops are late, a minority perfect, few unfaithful.
numbers: Stop Late 63.6%, Stop Perfectly 18.2%, Unfaithful but Correct Stop 3%; remainder in other categories, on the analysed sample.
limits: Small sample, one model, percentages read from one figure.
agent_relevance: Overthinking after the answer is more common than stopping too soon, so a stop rule is more likely to save cost than to lose accuracy.

source: Chen, Xu, Liang, et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: First broad measurement of overthinking. On '2+3' o1-like models used far more tokens than normal models. The first round of solutions is already correct in most cases; later rounds add little.
numbers: 1,953% more tokens than conventional models for 2+3. In over 92% of cases the first round of solutions is correct; the first round is under 60% of tokens. Self-training to shorten output cut MATH500 tokens 48.6% on QwQ-32B-Preview with accuracy kept.
limits: QwQ and R1 only; math sets (ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME). Their fix needs training.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and S0 spending by difficulty: easy items need a stop after the first solution.

source: Wang, Liu, Xu, et al. (2025) On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: The opposite failure: on hard problems models switch between thoughts too soon and do not finish a promising line. Incorrect answers use more tokens and more thought switches.
numbers: Incorrect responses use 225% more tokens than correct ones, with 418% more thought switching. A thought-switching penalty (TIP) at decoding raised accuracy on hard sets without fine-tuning.
limits: Hard math sets only. Shows a long output is not a sign of enough thinking.
agent_relevance: A stop rule must separate 'converged' from 'jumping around'.

source: Zhang, Lin, Hou, et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: RL teaches a reasoning model to choose between thinking and no-thinking per problem. NoThinking is the better choice on easy items.
numbers: On three math sets, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B response length down 53% and accuracy up 2.4%. A table row: accuracy 42.2, 1055 tokens, length -38.8%, +6.5 points on one benchmark.
limits: Needs RL training. Math only. 1.5B model.
agent_relevance: Supports the S0 gate: choose direct vs reasoning by class. The effect is class-dependent, so our S0 table must be measured.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi, Schwartz (2025) Don't Overthink It: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains
finding: Within one question, shorter sampled chains are more often right than the longest. Run k chains in parallel, halt when the first m finish, vote among them (short-m@k).
numbers: Shortest chain up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest for the same question. short-1@k matches or beats majority voting at low compute with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens; short-3@k beats majority voting at all budgets with up to 33% less wall time. Fine-tuning on short chains beat long and random chains.
limits: Reasoning models on math. Length-correctness link is within-question only.
agent_relevance: A zero-training stop rule: stop all attempts once the first few finish. Fits S3 with several short independent attempts (G11).

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Use token-level confidence over windows to drop low-confidence traces during generation (stop them early) and weight votes. Large token savings with similar or better accuracy.
numbers: Offline: GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025, DeepConf@512 = 99.9% vs 97.0% majority vote (cons@512) and 91.8% pass@1. Online: up to 84.7% fewer tokens. DeepConf-low cuts 43 to 79% of tokens on AIME24/25, BRUMO25, HMMT25; DeepConf-high saves 18 to 59%.
limits: Accuracy drops in a few settings (Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9; GPT-OSS-120B on HMMT25). Models can be confident and wrong, which the authors name as a key limitation. Needs logprobs.
agent_relevance: Stopping individual bad attempts on low confidence is a second form of termination. Confident-wrong traces mean confidence alone is not proof (G3).

source: Hu, Liu, Feng, et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT)
finding: UoT simulates future question-answer branches, scores questions by information gain, and picks one. It raises success of information seeking in 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting, and cuts the number of questions.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% across several LLMs vs direct prompting (Llama-3-70B, Claude-3-Opus, GPT-4 and others). Datasets: DX (104 dialogues, 5 test diseases), MedDG, FloDial, 20 Questions. One cell: GPT-4 with UoT 55.3 vs Llama3-70B direct 34.2 on Common 20Q (different models).
limits: Simulated answerer is GPT-4. It studies what to ask more than when to stop. The 38.1% is an average of relative gains.
agent_relevance: Information gain is a second 'enough' signal: stop when the candidate set collapses to one. Complements CaRT.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: With one variable missing, models can usually solve the full problem but often cannot pick the one question that unlocks it. The gap is knowing what is missing, not computing.
numbers: Near or above 80 to 90% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q (e.g. GPT-4o 99.34% in one GSME-Q setting) but only 40 to 50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q. Models: GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Gemma 2 2B/9B/27B. Gemma 2 2B scored 0.09 to 0.26% on Logic-Q in some settings. Solving the fully specified version was not enough.
limits: Multiple-choice question selection with one missing variable; real tasks may miss several. Only anecdotes for newer models (Gemini 2.5 Pro).
agent_relevance: 'Do I know enough?' is a separate skill from 'can I solve it'. The scaffold needs an explicit 'what is missing' step before any stop decision.

source: Comparison of Adaptive-Consistency and ESC (my reading)
finding: Both stop rules agree: stop when the answer distribution is concentrated. Adaptive-Consistency uses a Bayesian posterior over answer counts; ESC uses windows of identical answers.
numbers: ESC reports -80.1% samples on GSM8K; Adaptive-Consistency reports 3.3x (about -70%) for math. Different models, max budgets and data, so not comparable.
limits: Cross-paper reading, not a head-to-head experiment. No paper I opened ran both on one setup.
agent_relevance: Start with the simpler window rule; compare in our harness at equal tokens before keeping it (G7).

source: Synthesis of failure and boundary cases across opened papers
finding: Boundaries seen: (1) domain shift (CaRT OOD; probe logic-to-math); (2) hard tasks gain little (Answer Convergence on MATH/GPQA/AIME; ESC on MATH); (3) confident-wrong traces (DeepConf); (4) correlated samples break independence (Adaptive-Consistency); (5) code compresses little (DEER 19.9% vs 61.5%).
numbers: Numbers are from the individual lines above.
limits: My synthesis; no single study tests all five moderators.
agent_relevance: Use a conservative stop (full agreement plus an unfitted check) and re-validate per problem class.

source: Synthesis of rival explanations for why stopping helps
finding: Rival accounts: (a) answers converge early and later steps are redundant (Answer Convergence, Chen et al.); (b) long chains hurt, shorter chains are more correct (Hassid et al.); (c) late reflection adds noise (DEER); (d) bad runs switch thoughts too often (Wang et al., underthinking). No experiment cleanly separates these.
numbers: Hassid: shortest chain up to 34.5% more accurate than longest. Chen: first round correct in over 92% of cases. Wang: wrong runs use 225% more tokens.
limits: Length is confounded with difficulty. Hassid et al. control for this by comparing chains within one question.
agent_relevance: Do not stop on length alone. Compare attempts on the same item in code.

source: Evidence gap: no independent replication of CaRT found
finding: As of 2026-11-03 I found no independent replication of CaRT in the sources I opened. The Semantic Scholar citation page returned one partial list of 2026 citing papers (adaptive rerouting, tool granularity) and was then rate limited; arXiv and OpenAlex APIs were also blocked, so the forward-citation check is incomplete.
numbers: Partial list not opened further.
limits: Throttled APIs mean absence of evidence only.
agent_relevance: Treat CaRT-style learned stopping as [S]. Training-free stop rules (ESC, Adaptive-Consistency, answer agreement) have more independent support.
